title: What are the three ways to set a price, and when do you use each?
description: Pricing methods for case interviews. Ways to set a price once you know the floor and the ceiling. A checklist, a worked example and how to say it.
hook: The three ways to set a price are cost-plus (your cost plus a markup), competitor-based (match, undercut or charge a premium to rivals) and value-based (a share of the value the customer gets). Use cost-plus to find the floor, value to find the ceiling and competitors to decide where to land, then check the total profit at the volume you expect.
body:
When it helps

Use this in any pricing case once you know the floor and the ceiling and need to turn them into a number. Each method answers a different question, so a balanced answer uses all three.

The checklist

Cost-plus

  • Unit cost × (1 + target markup)
  • Answers: what is the lowest price that makes us money?

Competitor-based

  • Match, undercut or charge a premium
  • Answers: what will customers compare us with?

Value-based

  • A share of the value the customer gets
  • Answers: what is the most they would rationally pay?

Launch strategy

  • Skim: start high, lower later (new technology, early adopters)
  • Penetrate: start low to win share fast (network effects, high switching costs later)

An example: software for accountants

A start-up's software saves accountants five hours a month. The three methods give very different answers:

MethodLogicPrice a month
Cost-plus$8 cost per user + 50% markup$12
Competitor-basedRivals charge $20 to $30$20 to $30
Value-based5 hours × an assumed $30 an hour = $150 savedUp to $150

Cost-plus leaves most of the value on the table. A price near $40 would still be a bargain for the customer and earn far more than $12, though sitting above rivals means the client must show why its product is better. The gap between methods is the point: it shows how much room there is.

Then check total profit, not unit price

An illustrative filter costs $12 to make and deliver. A rival sells for $20. The client's filter saves customers $6 of maintenance, so value-based pricing suggests up to about $26.

  • At $20, selling 100,000 units, contribution is ($20 − $12) × 100,000 = $800,000.
  • At $24, contribution per unit rises to $12. If sales fall to 60,000, total contribution is $12 × 60,000 = $720,000.

The higher price earns more per unit but less in total. At $24 the client needs at least $800,000 ÷ $12 ≈ 66,700 units to match the $20 result, so it can afford to lose up to a third of its volume, and no more. Customers also have to believe in the $6 saving before they will pay for it.

How it sounds in an interview

"I'd look at the price from three sides: what it costs us, what rivals charge, and what it is worth to the customer. Cost gives a floor of $12 and value a ceiling of about $26. I'd test $24, but only if we keep at least two-thirds of the volume we'd sell at $20."

The weak version picks one method, usually "cost plus a healthy margin", and never mentions volume.

Common mistakes

  • Using cost-plus alone and leaving value on the table.
  • Treating value-based price as the answer, when customers may not believe or capture all the value.
  • Forgetting that a higher price changes volume.

Practise it

1. A product costs $40. The client wants a 25% markup. What price does cost-plus give, and what is the margin on that price?

Show the answer

Price: $40 × 1.25 = $50. Margin: $10 ÷ $50 = 20%. Markup is measured on cost, margin on price, which is why they differ.

2. A new console game is launching with strong fan demand. Skim or penetrate?

Show the answer

Usually skim: dedicated fans will pay full price at launch, and the price can come down later to reach more casual buyers. Penetration suits products where winning users early locks in value, such as platforms with network effects.
